This technical report provides an exhaustive legal, regulatory, financial, and jurisprudential audit of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive regime and provincial and territorial research and development (R&D) tax credits in Canada as of November 2026.

The Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential structural expansion in over a decade between March 2025 and November 2026. At the federal level, Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, enacted four major enhancements announced in Budget 2025: (1) doubling the annual SR&ED expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (increasing the maximum annual cash refund from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; (2) extending access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; (3) expanding the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million and introducing an alternative 3-year average gross revenue phase-out test over the $15 million–$75 million range; and (4) restoring the eligibility of depreciable capital expenditures (under reinstated paragraph 37(1)(b) of the Income Tax Act), leased equipment costs, and Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) acquired or incurred on or after December 16, 2024 (after December 15, 2024). Furthermore, Federal Budget 2026 proposes expanding SR&ED eligibility to include commercialisation expenditures—specifically regulatory approval and intellectual property (IP) protection costs—for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026. At the provincial level, Quebec abolished eight legacy R&D tax measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating them into the fully refundable CRIC regime offering 30% on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20% on excess amounts, including 100% of eligible capital equipment and 50% of subcontractor costs.

Practitioners and claimants must simultaneously navigate strict statutory compliance rules that frequently invalidate or reduce claims during CRA technical and financial reviews. Common compliance errors corrected in this report include: (a) applying an outdated 65% proxy overhead rate rather than the statutory 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4) (which has been 55% since 2014); (b) failing to apply the two-tier salary caps for specified employees (10% shareholders and non-arm's length employees), which limit direct SR&ED salary expenditures to 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under subsection 37(9.1) ($373,000 for 2026 based on the 2026 YMPE of $74,600) and limit the proxy salary base to the lesser of 75% of salary and 2.5 times the YMPE under Regulation 2900(7) ($186,500 for 2026); (c) misidentifying the statutory provisions for government assistance and contract payment reductions, which sit in subsections 127(11.1) and 127(18) and paragraph 37(1)(d) rather than subsection 37(2) (which governs foreign R&D); and (d) relying on taxpayer relief under subsection 220(3.1) to cure a missed 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m), a deadline that is absolute and admits of no ministerial or judicial extension.
1. Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Core Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program is jointly structured by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates tax policy and drafts legislative amendments, and administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which oversees technical eligibility reviews, financial audits, policy publications, and tax credit assessments. Unlike discretionary government grant programmes, the SR&ED regime is an entitlement-based statutory mechanism embedded directly within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and Income Tax Regulations (ITR). Provided a taxpayer satisfies the substantive technical criteria, expenditure qualification rules, and mandatory filing deadlines, the Minister of National Revenue is statutorily bound to allow the deduction and issue the corresponding Investment Tax Credit (ITC).
The statutory architecture operates across four primary pillars of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations:

items: Definitional Scope (ITA Subsection 248(1)): Establishes the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development," enumerating the three core categories of eligible investigation—basic research under paragraph (a), applied research under paragraph (b), and experimental development under paragraph (c)—alongside the eight categories of eligible support work under paragraph (d) and the seven absolute statutory exclusions under paragraphs (e) through (k). Subsection 248(1) also defines critical operational terms including "salary or wages," "specified employee," "specified shareholder," and "prescribed".

Expenditure Deduction Pool (ITA Section 37 and Regulations 2900 & 2902): Governs the accumulation and deduction of allowable SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada under subsection 37(1), including current expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a) and reinstated capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b). Subsection 37(2) separately addresses research and development carried on outside Canada. Subsection 37(1.1) establishes the 10% cap on permissible salaries for Canadian-resident employees performing SR&ED outside Canada in support of a Canadian project. Subsection 37(8) and Regulation 2900(2) define expenditures "all or substantially all" (ASA) or "directly attributable" to SR&ED under the Traditional Method versus the Proxy Method. Subsections 37(9) through 37(9.4) impose restrictions and YMPE caps on remuneration paid to specified employees. Subsection 37(10) governs the irrevocable annual election to use the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method. Subsections 37(11) and 37(12) enforce the mandatory 12-month post-filing-due-date reporting deadline for prescribed forms and prescribed information.

Investment Tax Credit Computation and Reductions (ITA Subsections 127(5) to 127(36) and Regulation 4600): Subsection 127(5) authorizes the deduction of ITCs against Part I tax otherwise payable. Subsection 127(9) defines "investment tax credit," "qualified expenditure," "government assistance," "non-government assistance," and "contract payment," and contains paragraph 127(9)(m), which bars any expenditure from entering the ITC calculation if the prescribed form containing prescribed information is not filed within 12 months of the taxpayer's filing-due date. Subsections 127(10.1) to 127(10.6) govern the enhanced 35% ITC addition (+20% on top of the 15% base rate) and the allocation of the $6 million expenditure limit among associated corporations. Subsections 127(11.1), 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) mandate the reduction of qualified expenditures by government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments. Subsection 127(11.2) establishes the "available for use" timing rule for capital acquisitions. Subsection 127(11.6) restricts non-arm's length expenditures to the supplier's cost. Subsection 127(13) permits non-arm's length transfers of qualified contract expenditures via Form T1146. Subsection 127(26) deems unpaid non-salary SR&ED expenditures not incurred if unpaid 180 days after year-end (paralleling subsection 78(4) for unpaid salaries). Subsections 127(27) to 127(36) govern the 20-year ITC recapture regime when SR&ED property or transformed materials are sold or converted to commercial use.

Refundable Investment Tax Credit Mechanics (ITA Section 127.1): Defines "qualifying corporation" and "qualifying income limit" under subsection 127.1(2) and establishes the statutory mechanism under subsection 127.1(1) by which unused ITCs earned by qualifying CCPCs, ECPCs, individuals, and certain trusts are deemed paid on account of Part I tax and refunded in cash by the CRA.

body.text: 1.2 Enacted Reforms under Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 (Royal Assent: March 26, 2026)

Following consultations initiated by the Department of Finance in 2024 and proposals announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and tabled in Parliament in the 2025 Federal Budget on November 4, 2025, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, First Session, Forty-fifth Parliament, Statutes of Canada 2026, Chapter 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Bill C-15 enacted the most sweeping expansion of the SR&ED program since the 2012 budget cuts, reversing the 2014 elimination of capital expenditures and significantly expanding access to the 35% refundable credit.

Practitioners must carefully distinguish the statutory effective dates ("in-force" rules) under Bill C-15, as three of the measures apply based on when a corporation's taxation year begins, whereas the restoration of capital expenditures applies based on the date the property is acquired or the lease cost is incurred:

items: Doubling the Enhanced 35% Expenditure Limit to $6 Million (Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024): For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (after December 15, 2024), the maximum annual expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. Because current SR&ED expenditures within the expenditure limit are 100% refundable for qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), the maximum annual cash refund at the 35% rate doubled from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000.

Extension of the Enhanced 35% Refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) (Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024): Prior to Bill C-15, public corporations resident in Canada (and private corporations controlled by public corporations) were strictly limited to the 15% non-refundable basic ITC, causing startups that went public on a stock exchange to immediately lose their 35% refundable SR&ED credits. Bill C-15 established a new corporate classification—Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)—granting qualifying Canadian-resident public corporations (and their eligible subsidiaries) access to the 35% ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures, with 100% refundability on current expenditures and 40% refundability on capital expenditures up to the expenditure limit. For qualified expenditures exceeding the $6 million expenditure limit, an ECPC earns the 15% basic ITC on a non-refundable (0% refund) basis.

Broadened Phase-Out Thresholds ($15M to $75M) and the Gross Revenue Grind Election (Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024): Under the prior rules, a CCPC's $3 million expenditure limit began phasing out once prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada across the associated group reached $10 million and was completely eliminated at $50 million. Under Bill C-15, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range is expanded to $15,000,000 to $75,000,000. For an ECPC, the $6 million expenditure limit phases out based solely on its average annual gross revenue over the preceding 3 fiscal years over the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 range. Crucially, Bill C-15 also permits CCPCs to elect (using the prescribed form) to have their expenditure limit phase-out computed using the 3-year average gross revenue test ($15M to $75M) instead of the taxable capital test—a major planning advantage for capital-intensive biotechnology, clean technology, and hardware manufacturing CCPCs that hold over $15 million in balance sheet capital but generate less than $15 million in gross revenue.

Restoration of SR&ED Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs (Property Acquired or Lease Costs Incurred After December 15, 2024): After an 11-year hiatus (capital expenditures having been eliminated effective January 1, 2014), Bill C-15 reinstated paragraph 37(1)(b) of the Income Tax Act and amended subsection 127(9) to restore eligibility for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (after December 15, 2024), as well as equipment lease costs incurred on or after December 16, 2024. Eligible capital expenditures qualify for both immediate 100% income deductibility via the section 37(1) pool and the SR&ED ITC (at 35% up to the $6M expenditure limit, refundable at 40%, and 15% above the limit). Both whole capital expenditures (where the property is intended to be used all or substantially all [ASA, ≥90%] of its operating time over its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada, or have ≥90% of its value consumed in SR&ED) and Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) (used primarily [>50%] for SR&ED, claimed at 25% in the first term and 25% in the second term) are restored.

body.text: 1.3 Proposed Reforms under Federal Budget 2026 (Commercialisation, IP Protection, and Regulatory Approvals)

Building on the Bill C-15 legislative overhaul, Canada's 2026 Federal Budget (Masters of our Destiny, PDF pp. 127, 420–421) announced a second wave of structural SR&ED reforms aimed at bridging Canada's commercialisation gap and retaining domestic intellectual property. Specifically, Budget 2026 proposes to expand eligible SR&ED expenditures to include specific commercialisation costs closely tied to eligible SR&ED projects, namely expenditures incurred for regulatory approvals and intellectual property (IP) protection. General marketing or commercial production costs unrelated to qualifying SR&ED activities remain excluded under subsection 248(1).

The proposed commercialisation expansion applies to expenditures incurred in taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026 (Budget Day), subject to legislative enactment, and is projected by the Department of Finance to deliver $930 million in support over five years, with $235 million ongoing annually. To prevent tax-subsidized IP stripping, Budget 2026 (p. 421) proposes specific recapture rules whereby, if a taxpayer subsequently disposes of intellectual property in respect of which SR&ED tax incentives were claimed for IP protection costs, both the related section 37 SR&ED pool deduction and the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit will be subject to recapture. In addition, the CRA is mandated under Budget 2026 (p. 127) to publish sector-specific administrative guidance clarifying SR&ED eligibility and the nexus required for commercialisation expenses.
2. Substantive Technical Eligibility: Subsection 248(1), the "Why" and "How" Requirements, and Statutory Exclusions
2.1 The Three Categories of Pure SR&ED (Subsection 248(1) Paragraphs (a), (b), and (c))

Entitlement to SR&ED tax incentives begins with the threshold question of whether the underlying technical activities satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (rather than section 127, which governs expenditure quantification once technical eligibility is established). Under the preamble of subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" falling into one of three foundational categories:

items: Basic Research (Paragraph (a)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, such as fundamental laboratory research investigating natural phenomena purely to expand theoretical scientific understanding.

Applied Research (Paragraph (b)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, provided systematic experimentation or analysis is actually performed to test the formulated hypotheses, as emphasized by the Tax Court of Canada in Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 21.

Experimental Development (Paragraph (c)): Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development under paragraph (c) encompasses the vast majority of industrial SR&ED claims in Canada across software engineering, advanced manufacturing, materials science, chemical process engineering, agricultural technology, and hardware development.

body.text: 2.2 The Eight Categories of Eligible Support Work (Subsection 248(1) Paragraph (d))

Recognizing that pure experimental development or scientific research cannot be conducted in a vacuum, paragraph (d) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) extends eligibility to work with respect to eight exhaustive categories of support activities: (1) engineering; (2) design; (3) operations research; (4) mathematical analysis; (5) computer programming; (6) data collection; (7) testing; and (8) psychological research.

Work within these eight categories never qualifies for SR&ED on a standalone basis (except where a non-arm's length performer is contracted solely for support work under special NAL rules). To qualify under paragraph (d), the support work must satisfy a strict two-part statutory nexus test. First, the activity must be performed directly in support of basic research (paragraph (a)), applied research (paragraph (b)), or experimental development (paragraph (c)) undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Second, the scale, volume, and duration of the engineering, coding, data collection, or testing must be commensurate with the needs of that underlying basic research, applied research, or experimental development. Sweeping in commercial user-interface coding, routine quality assurance testing, or general data ingestion violates the commensurate test and triggers audit disallowance.
2.3 The Seven Statutory Exclusions (Subsection 248(1) Paragraphs (e) to (k))

Even where a project involves genuine experimental development, paragraphs (e) through (k) of subsection 248(1) explicitly carve out and exclude seven categories of commercial, routine, or non-scientific activities. Importantly, these exclusions only carve out routine or commercial work from a project that already contains SR&ED; they do not automatically invalidate the eligible core of the project.

body.text: 2.4 Evolution of CRA Eligibility Guidance: From IC 86-4R3 and the "Five Questions" to the "Two Requirements" ("Why" and "How")

A thorough understanding of CRA technical reviews requires tracing the evolution of the agency's administrative guidelines, all of which interpret the unchanged statutory text of subsection 248(1). Prior to 1985, Interpretation Bulletin IT-439 provided brief guidance on "scientific research". In May 1985, Department of Finance Budget Papers added the term "experimental development" to clarify that routine engineering was excluded while industrial experimental development was included. Following a March 4, 1986 Department of Finance clarification, Revenue Canada and industry specialists published Information Circular 86-4 in 1986 (culminating in IC 86-4R3 in 1994), which established the three classic industrial SR&ED pillars: (1) Scientific or Technological Advancement, (2) Scientific or Technological Uncertainty, and (3) Scientific and Technical Content (systematic investigation).

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (1998), Judge Bowman synthesized IC 86-4R3 and subsection 248(1) into a five-criterion judicial test. In 2012 (revised in 2015), the CRA codified Judge Bowman's framework into the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy as the Five Questions. Following a 2020 modernization initiative, the CRA in summer 2021 archived the 2015 policy and published the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, which consolidates the Five Questions into Two Requirements: The "Why" Requirement and The "How" Requirement. Both frameworks remain actively used in tandem—the CRA's Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) structure their eligibility reviews around the Two Requirements, while the Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal evaluate appeals under the Five Questions from Northwest Hydraulic.

The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty — Mapping to Northwest Hydraulic Questions 1 and 4): To satisfy the "Why" requirement, the work must be undertaken to resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty (Question 1) for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement (Question 4). Scientific or technological uncertainty exists when whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, is not known or cannot be determined on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience. Uncertainty must be objective—existing at the level of a competent professional in the field—not merely a subjective knowledge gap of the claimant's internal team. Crucially, Canadian jurisprudence and CRA policy recognize "system uncertainty" (originally articulated in IC 86-4R3 para. 4.8 and upheld in 1726437 Ontario Inc. o/a Airmax Technologies v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 376, and A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 48): even where individual components or technologies are well known, integrating them into a complex system under tight geometric, pressure, thermal, or performance constraints can generate non-trivial technological uncertainty as to how the components will interact. Conversely, technical problems solvable by standard procedures, trial-and-error parameter tuning, or routine engineering do not qualify. The investigation must seek to generate new scientific or technological knowledge that advances general understanding in the field beyond what was available to competent practitioners at the outset of the project. A new commercial product or software feature is not itself an advancement; the advancement is the underlying technological knowledge gained. Importantly, failure to achieve the technical or commercial objective does not disqualify a project—proving through systematic experimentation that a plausible hypothesis fails eliminates a technological pathway and thereby generates eligible technological knowledge (Northwest Hydraulic, 98 D.T.C. 1839; RIS-Christie Ltd., 99 D.T.C. 5087; A&D Precision, 2019 TCC 48).

The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search — Mapping to Northwest Hydraulic Questions 2, 3, and 5): To satisfy the "How" requirement, the claimant must conduct a structured systematic investigation or search by means of experiment or analysis. Under Question 2, the claimant must observe the problem, define a clear technical objective, articulate the specific uncertainty, and formulate one or more testable hypotheses (ideas consistent with known scientific facts set up specifically to be proved or disproved) aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty; randomly trying options until one works without a hypothesis fails Question 2. Under Question 3, the claimant must follow the discipline of the scientific method, setting objectives and indicators early, executing planned experiments or analyses to test the hypothesis, measuring results, drawing logical conclusions, and iteratively modifying the hypothesis across sequential tests (Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88; National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47). Under Question 5, a detailed record of the hypotheses formulated, test protocols executed, and results obtained must be maintained contemporaneously as the work progresses—not reconstructed retroactively at claim preparation time (Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6; National R&D Inc., 2020 TCC 47).
3. Federal SR&ED Financial Incentives: Deductible Pool, ITC Rates, Thresholds, and Refundability
3.1 The Section 37(1) Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

The first financial incentive under the federal SR&ED program is the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures governed by subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act (computed in Part 3, Section C of Form T661). All allowable current SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada under paragraph 37(1)(a) and allowable capital SR&ED expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024 under paragraph 37(1)(b)—net of government and non-government assistance, contract payments, and prior-year federal SR&ED ITCs applied or refunded (which reduce the pool in the subsequent taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e))—enter a cumulative tax pool.

A taxpayer may deduct any portion (up to 100%) of the positive year-end balance of its section 37(1) pool in computing net income for tax purposes in the current taxation year (reported on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), or elect to leave all or part of the pool balance undeducted and carry it forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in any future taxation year. This indefinite carryforward is particularly valuable for early-stage R&D corporations: rather than creating non-capital losses that expire after 20 years, preserving expenditures in the section 37(1) pool prevents clock expiration until the corporation achieves commercial profitability.

By contrast, R&D expenditures carried on outside Canada (other than permissible Canadian-resident employee salaries within the 10% cap under subsection 37(1.1)) are governed by subsection 37(2): they are deductible as current expenses in the year incurred in computing business income, but they do not enter the section 37(1) carryforward pool and do not earn federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credits.

3.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out ("Grind") Mechanics and Qualifying Income Limits

Under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.3) of the Income Tax Act, the maximum annual $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit for the enhanced 35% ITC must be shared among all associated corporations within a corporate group via Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). Ignoring the association rules and failing to file Schedule T2SCH49 before claiming is a frequent compliance error.
3.3.1 The Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas (Post-December 15, 2024 vs. Pre-December 16, 2024)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (under Bill C-15), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced ("ground down") on a straight-line basis as the corporate group's size metric rises from $15,000,000 to $75,000,000. Under the default Prior-Year Taxable Capital Employed in Canada test for CCPCs, if the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and its associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year is $15,000,000 or less, the expenditure limit is the full $6,000,000. (Prior to Bill C-15, for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3,000,000 expenditure limit phased out over the $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 taxable capital range).

Under the Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Test—which is mandatory for an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) and elective for any CCPC that files the prescribed election—the $6,000,000 expenditure limit phases out over the exact same $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 range based on the average annual gross revenue of the corporation (and associated corporations) over the last 3 fiscal years.
3.3.2 The Qualifying Income Limit Formula (Section 127.1(2))

While prior-year taxable income does not reduce the $6,000,000 expenditure limit itself, prior-year taxable income determines whether a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2). Both a "qualifying corporation" CCPC and a "non-qualifying" CCPC (whose prior-year taxable income exceeded its Qualifying Income Limit) receive 100% refundability on the 35% ITC for current expenditures up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit (and 40% refundability on capital expenditures up to the limit). However, for qualified expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 expenditure limit (which earn the 15% basic ITC), a qualifying corporation CCPC receives a 40% cash refund on that 15% ITC (an effective 6% cash refund on excess spend), whereas a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income exceeded its Qualifying Income Limit receives 0% refundability above the expenditure limit.

Per the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), a CCPC's Qualifying Income Limit is $500,000 (calculated prior to specified future tax consequences), reduced as prior-year taxable capital rises. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the formula is:

Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is ≤ $10,000,000, or the lesser of $40,000,000 and the taxable capital exceeding $10,000,000. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the formula is: Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000]
where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is ≤ $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the taxable capital exceeding $15,000,000.
3.3.3 Worked Numerical Example of Post-Bill C-15 ITC and Refundability

Consider a qualifying CCPC with $8,000,000 in current qualified SR&ED expenditures in its taxation year ending December 31, 2026, with prior-year taxable income below the $500,000 qualifying income limit and prior-year taxable capital below the $15,000,000 phase-out threshold. On the first $6,000,000 within the expenditure limit, the corporation earns the enhanced rate of $6,000,000 × 35% = $2,100,000 ITC, which is 100% refundable ($2,100,000 cash refund). On the remaining $2,000,000 above the expenditure limit, the corporation earns the basic rate of $2,000,000 × 15% = $300,000 ITC, which for a qualifying CCPC is 40% refundable (40% × $300,000 = $120,000 cash refund) and 60% non-refundable ($180,000 available to offset Part I tax or carry back 3 years / carry forward 20 years). In total, the CCPC earns $2,400,000 in ITCs, of which $2,220,000 is refunded in cash. If the claimant were an ECPC instead of a qualifying CCPC, it would still receive the full $2,100,000 cash refund on the first $6,000,000, while the $300,000 ITC on the excess $2,000,000 would be 0% refundable and entirely applied against Part I tax or carried over.
3.4 Carryback, Carryforward, and Taxation of Federal ITCs

Under subsection 127(9), any non-refundable portion of a federal SR&ED ITC (or any refundable portion that the taxpayer does not receive as a cash refund) that is not deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable in the current year may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years.

Under paragraph 37(1)(e) of the Income Tax Act, a federal SR&ED ITC claimed to reduce Part I tax or received as a cash refund for a given taxation year reduces the section 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year (and if the reduction exceeds the pool balance in that following year, the excess is included in business income). Crucially, unlike government grants or CRA-administered provincial R&D tax credits (which reduce qualified expenditures in the current year under subsection 127(11.1)), the federal SR&ED ITC only impacts the deductible pool in the subsequent taxation year and never reduces the current year's qualified expenditures.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Election Methods, and Specific Cost Rules
4.1 Traditional Method vs. Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method

A foundational strategic decision on every SR&ED claim is the annual choice between the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method (the Proxy Method) and the Traditional Method for capturing SR&ED overhead expenditures. Under subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant elects the Proxy Method by ticking Line 160 in Part 1 of Form T661 and completing Part 5 (entering "0" on Line 360). To use the Traditional Method, the claimant ticks Line 162 and reports actual SR&ED overhead on Line 360 (entering "0" on Lines 355 and 502 and skipping Part 5). The election applies to the entire claim for that taxation year, can be changed from year to year, and must be made on the first Form T661 filed for the year. Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice between the Proxy Method and Traditional Method is strictly irrevocable for that taxation year. If no valid election is made by the 18-month filing deadline under subsection 37(11), the Traditional Method applies automatically by default.

Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA is equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base. Practitioners must beware of outdated summaries claiming a 65% proxy rate: the PPA rate was 65% for 2012 and prior years, 60% for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% since January 1, 2014. The PPA (reported on Line 820 of Part 5 and carried to Line 502 of Part 4 of Form T661) is a purely notional amount. It is added to qualified SR&ED expenditures solely to earn the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (yielding an additional 55% × 35% = 19.25% effective refundable credit on every dollar of eligible base salary for a qualifying CCPC or ECPC). The PPA cannot be added to the section 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the actual underlying overhead expenses (office supplies, utilities, support staff wages, cloud hosting, software subscriptions, property taxes, maintenance) remain deductible as ordinary business expenses.

Under subsection 2900(6) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, the PPA cannot exceed the claimant's overall business deduction ceiling, computed via the formula A − B − C. In this formula, A is the total amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold); B is the sum of specified statutory deductions identified in the Regulations, such as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA), the section 37 SR&ED deduction on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1, interest, and deductions under sections 20, 24, 26, 30, 32, 37, 66–66.8, and 104; and C is building rent and building maintenance/use expenditures. The overall cap typically does not restrict the PPA provided non-excluded business deductions (other than SR&ED salary itself) are at least $55 for every $100 of salary in the proxy base.

body.text: 4.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, YMPE Caps, and Foreign R&D Labour

Salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED represent the largest expenditure component of most Canadian claims. Under subsection 248(1), "salary or wages" means income from an office or employment (reported on a T4 slip), plus the employer's share of statutory payroll deductions (such as CPP/QPP and EI).
4.2.1 The "All or Substantially All" (ASA ≥90%) Salary Rule

Under Regulation 2900(5), if an arm's length (non-specified) employee spends all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) of their working time in the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED activities, 100% of their eligible salary or wages is deemed to be an SR&ED expenditure and enters the proxy salary base. If the employee spends less than 90% of their time on SR&ED, only the exact proportion of time directly engaged in eligible SR&ED activities (substantiated by contemporaneous time tracking and technical logs) can be claimed.
4.2.2 Specified Employees: Definition, Ownership Attribution, and Two-Tier YMPE Caps

Strict statutory anti-avoidance caps apply to "specified employees"—which includes almost all startup founders, owner-managers, and family members working in a private business. Under subsection 248(1), a "specified employee" is an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, sibling, parent, or child of a controlling shareholder) OR who is a "specified shareholder" of the employer. A "specified shareholder" is a taxpayer who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time during the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the employer or of any corporation related to the employer.

In applying the 10% ownership test under subsection 248(1), shares owned by any person not dealing at arm's length with the individual count as the individual's shares; shares held via a partnership or fixed trust count in proportion to the individual's interest; and a beneficiary of a discretionary family trust is treated as owning 100% of the trust's shares. Because the statutory test applies "at any time during the year," a founder who owns 10% or more on the first day of the fiscal year and is diluted below 10% after a financing round during the year remains a specified employee for that entire taxation year.
Two separate statutory caps apply to every specified employee:

items: Direct SR&ED Salary Expenditure Cap (ITA Subsection 37(9.1) — 5 × YMPE): Under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages (Lines 305 + 309 of Form T661) that can be claimed for a specified employee (under both the Traditional and Proxy methods) cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee (days ÷ 365). If the specified employee performs SR&ED for two or more associated corporations, the single 5 × YMPE ceiling must be shared across the group by filing Form T1174 under subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.4); if the associated corporations fail to file Form T1174, none of the specified employee's salary qualifies in any associated corporation.

Proxy Salary Base Cap (Regulation 2900(7) & 2900(8) — Lesser of 75% of Total Salary and 2.5 × YMPE): When computing the Salary Base in Part 5 of Form T661 for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount, Regulation 2900(7) imposes a second, lower ceiling on each specified employee equal to the lesser of: (a) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages from the employer for the year (meaning even if a founder spends 100% of their time on SR&ED, at most 75% of their salary can enter the proxy base), and (b) 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year (days ÷ 365). Under Regulation 2900(8), associated corporations share a single 2.5 × YMPE proxy base cap for the same specified employee.

body.text: To illustrate, suppose a CCPC owner-manager (a specified employee) is paid a regular salary of $200,000 in the taxation year ending December 31, 2026, with no bonuses, and spends 80% of their time directly on eligible SR&ED. The direct SR&ED salary claimed on Line 305 is 80% × $200,000 = $160,000, which is below the 2026 subsection 37(9.1) cap of $373,000 and is therefore allowed in full. However, for the proxy salary base addition in Part 5, Regulation 2900(7) caps the inclusion at the lesser of actual SR&ED salary ($160,000), 75% × $200,000 = $150,000, and 2.5 × $74,600 = $186,500. Because the 75% test bites first, only $150,000 enters the proxy salary base, generating a 55% PPA of $150,000 × 55% = $82,500.
4.2.3 Remuneration Exclusions: Dividends, Bonuses, Taxable Benefits, and Unpaid Wages (180-Day Rule)

Dividends paid to shareholder-founders are returns on share capital reported on T5 slips, not employment income under subsection 248(1). Dividends never qualify as SR&ED expenditures ($0 deductible pool, $0 PPA, $0 ITC), and unpaid founders who receive zero salary cannot claim their time regardless of hours worked. For specified employees, subsection 37(9) strictly excludes all bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits (under sections 6 and 7 of the ITA) from both direct SR&ED expenditures and the proxy salary base. Furthermore, under Regulation 2900(9), bonuses, profit-based pay, and sections 6/7 taxable benefits are excluded from the proxy salary base for all employees (not only specified employees).

Under subsection 78(4) (and subsection 127(26)), accrued salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that are not actually paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year must be reported on Line 315 of Form T661 and deducted from current-year allowable SR&ED expenditures. When the corporation subsequently pays those accrued wages in a later taxation year, the amount may be claimed as a direct SR&ED salary expenditure on Line 310 in the year of payment, but under Regulation 2900(9) and the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, late-paid prior-year salary claimed on Line 310 is permanently excluded from the proxy salary base. Timely remittance of payroll source deductions (income tax, CPP, and EI, noting that for 2026 CPP is 5.95% up to $74,600 capping at $4,230.45 each, plus CPP2 up to $416 each on earnings up to $85,000, while founders controlling >40% of voting shares are EI-exempt) is the CRA's primary audit evidence of timely salary payment.
4.2.4 Permissible Salary for SR&ED Performed Outside Canada (Subsection 37(1.1) — The 10% Rule)

While general foreign R&D under subsection 37(2) does not earn ITCs, subsection 37(1.1) of the Income Tax Act allows a claimant to include "permissible salary or wages" for SR&ED performed outside Canada on Line 307 (non-specified employees) and Line 309 (specified employees) of Form T661, provided five mandatory conditions are satisfied:

items: The SR&ED work outside Canada was directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant and not performed by an independent contractor;
The employee was a resident of Canada at the time the salary expense was incurred;
The work was directly related to a business of the claimant;
The work carried out outside Canada was an integral part and solely in support of an SR&ED project carried on inside Canada; and
The salary or wages paid were not subject to income or profits tax from another country.

body.text: Permissible foreign SR&ED salary is capped at the lesser of Amount A (total eligible foreign SR&ED salaries on Lines 307 + 309, subject to the 5 × YMPE cap for specified employees) and Amount B. Under the Proxy Method, Amount B is 10% of Line 306 (total salary or wages claimed for SR&ED performed in Canada). Under the Traditional Method, Amount B is 10% of the sum of Line 306 PLUS eligible salaries of employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED in Canada claimed as overhead on Line 360.
4.3 Subcontractors (Contract Expenditures) vs. Third-Party Payments

Payments to external parties for R&D in Canada fall into three distinct statutory categories under the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy and Third-Party Payments Policy (both updated March 30, 2022):

items: Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts (ITA Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) — Form T661 Line 340): When a claimant contracts an arm's length taxable Canadian supplier to perform SR&ED on the claimant's behalf in Canada, 100% of the eligible contract cost enters the section 37(1) deductible pool, and 80% of the eligible contract amount qualifies as a qualified expenditure for the SR&ED ITC under subsection 127(9). Under this 80% statutory inclusion rule, for arm's length contracts that are strictly for SR&ED, the CRA will not "look through" the contract to audit the contractor's underlying component expenses, except under subsections 37(14) and 37(15) where the contract includes non-current property. If the arm's length contractor is hired for pure SR&ED (basic research, applied research, or experimental development), the contractor may also file its own SR&ED claim for its expenditures, but the contractor must reduce its qualified SR&ED expenditures by the gross contract payment received or receivable under subsection 127(18) to prevent duplication of ITCs. Conversely, if an arm's length contractor is hired for support work only under paragraph 248(1)(d), the payer can claim the 80% contract expenditure (provided it directly supports the payer's pure SR&ED in Canada), but the performer cannot claim expenditures for the support work because support work on its own does not meet the definition of SR&ED.

Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Form T661 Line 345 and Form T1146): When a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length party, the expenditures are allowable in the payer's section 37(1) deductible pool (reported on Line 345), but 0% is a qualified expenditure for the payer's ITC. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own qualified SR&ED expenditures (and the amount received from the NAL payer is not considered a contract payment reducing the NAL performer's qualified expenditures). Alternatively, under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and payer may jointly file prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer all or part of the NAL performer's qualified expenditures (capped at the contract amount) to the payer. Subsection 127(24) is an anti-avoidance rule that prevents a claimant from circumventing the NAL rules by inserting an arm's length intermediary between itself and a NAL subcontractor.

Third-Party Payments (ITA Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and 37(1)(a)(ii) — Form T661 Line 370 and Form T1263): Third-party payments are payments made to specific categories of entities (Entities A through F: corporations resident in Canada [Entity A], approved associations [Entity B], approved universities, colleges, or research institutes [Entity C], non-profit SR&ED corporations exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j) [Entities D and F], and approved granting councils [Entity E]) to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to a business of the claimant, where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results. While public Canadian universities and affiliated colleges are automatically considered approved, non-affiliated colleges, research institutes, and associations must hold written approval from the Minister of National Revenue through the CRA Income Tax Rulings Directorate. Like arm's length contracts, 100% of an eligible third-party payment enters the section 37(1) pool and 80% enters qualified expenditures for ITC purposes, and claimants must retain documentation supporting Form T1263.

body.text: 4.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and the 20-Year ITC Recapture Regime

Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the Income Tax Act, paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations, and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), "materials for SR&ED" must be physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or items (solid, liquid, or gaseous) that compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is carried out or that results from the SR&ED at a given moment in the process. Both categories are 100% deductible in the section 37(1) pool and 100% eligible for the ITC under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, and can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the material is actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (not when purchased into inventory).

Materials Consumed (Form T661 Line 320) are materials destroyed, disposed of as waste, or rendered virtually valueless during SR&ED testing. The claimable laid-down cost includes invoice cost, customs and excise duties, freight, storage, and third-party preparation services (such as galvanizing metal parts prior to destructive testing). If the claimant manufactures the test materials internally (such as cardboard boxes produced in-house for a printing experiment), the claimable cost includes raw materials, direct labour, and a reasonable share of production overhead—even under the Proxy Method, provided manufacturing the material itself did not involve SR&ED. Process water that becomes part of a product and energy integral to a chemical reaction (or that is the subject of SR&ED) also qualify as materials consumed, whereas utility water and energy used to operate equipment or maintain ambient building temperatures do not. Materials Transformed (Form T661 Line 325) are raw materials or component parts incorporated into an experimental prototype, custom product, or commercial asset that retains value after the SR&ED testing concludes. If materials, goods, or services are purchased from a non-arm's length supplier, subsection 127(11.6) restricts the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes to the actual cost incurred by the NAL supplier (excluding any profit markup), with the adjustment entered on Line 543 of Form T661.
4.4.1 The 20-Year ITC Recapture Regime (ITA Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

When a taxpayer claims an SR&ED ITC on materials transformed, restored capital property (paragraph 37(1)(b)), Shared-Use-Equipment, or property acquired under an SR&ED contract, and within 20 taxation years of acquiring the property (extended from 10 years in paragraph 127(27)(a)) the taxpayer disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use, the ITC Recapture Rules in subsections 127(27) to 127(36) apply. Under subsection 127(27) (or subsection 127(28) for partnerships), the taxpayer must add back to its Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion an amount equal to the lesser of the original SR&ED ITC earned on the property (or transformed materials) and the applicable ITC percentage applied to the proceeds of disposition (if sold at arm's length) or the fair market value of the property (or transformed materials) when converted to commercial use or transferred to a non-arm's length party. Additionally, when SR&ED capital property is sold, Line 440 of Form T661 reduces the section 37(1) deductible pool by the lesser of the proceeds of disposition and the undeducted expenditure balance for that property in the prior-year pool; any excess proceeds up to original cost trigger Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) recapture included in income on Schedule T2SCH1, and any proceeds above original cost are treated as a capital gain.
4.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under Bill C-15 and the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (published June 29, 2026), SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (published June 8, 2026), and SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (published May 22, 2026), capital assets and leased equipment acquired or incurred after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024) qualify under three distinct mechanisms:

items: Full SR&ED Capital Expenditures (ITA Paragraph 37(1)(b) — Form T661 Line 390, Lines 262–263, and Part 6B Boxes 780, 782, 786): To qualify on Line 390, the claimant must acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024 with the demonstrable intent at the time of acquisition to either: (a) use the property for all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time throughout its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada; or (b) consume ASA (≥90%) of its value in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. While both new and used depreciable property meeting the ASA test can enter the section 37(1)(b) deductible pool, used equipment (or refurbished used equipment) is a "prescribed expenditure" under Regulation 2902(b) and is excluded from "qualified expenditures" for ITC purposes. Buildings, land, leasehold interests in buildings, goodwill, and non-depreciable assets are strictly excluded under paragraph 37(8)(d), and under the Proxy Method, general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF) is also excluded. Claimants must enter the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED properties per project on Lines 262–263 of Part 2, and report the 20 most expensive capital expenditures across the claim in Part 6B (Box 780: Property Name; Box 782: Full Capital Cost including purchase price, installation, customs/excise duties, and transportation; Box 786: Comma-separated Project Numbers).

Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) (Form T661 Line 504 and Part 6C Boxes 788, 790, 792): When new depreciable machinery or equipment (excluding GPOEF) acquired after December 15, 2024 is used primarily (more than 50%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada (but less than the 90% ASA threshold), it qualifies as Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9) and Regulation 2900(3). The claimant includes 25% of the capital cost in qualified expenditures on Line 504 in the first period (first-term SUE) and an additional 25% of the capital cost in the second period (second-term SUE), for a cumulative 50% of capital cost earning the ITC across the two periods. Details of the 20 most expensive SUE properties are reported in Part 6C (Box 788: Name; Box 790: Purchase Date; Box 792: 25% of Capital Cost).

Leased Equipment Costs (Form T661 Lines 350 & 355 and Part 6A Box 759): For equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, Line 350 captures 100% of lease costs for equipment used ASA (≥90%) for SR&ED in Canada (under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, excluding GPOEF under Proxy), while Line 355 (Proxy Method Only) captures 50% (half) of the lease cost for equipment used primarily (≥50% to <90%) for SR&ED in Canada (excluding GPOEF). The sum of Lines 350 and 355 must equal Box 759 in Part 6A.

body.text: 4.5.1 The Subsection 127(11.2) "Available for Use" Timing Opportunity for Pre-December 16, 2024 Orders

A notable technical timing interaction arises under subsection 127(11.2) of the Income Tax Act, as amended by Bill C-15. While the in-force provision for paragraph 37(1)(b) states that capital deductibility applies to property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, amended subsection 127(11.2) explicitly states that in applying subsections 127(5), (7), (8), paragraphs (a) and (a.1) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), and section 127.1, qualified property and first-term SUE are deemed not to have been acquired—and expenditures incurred to acquire property described in paragraph 37(1)(b) are deemed not to have been incurred—before the property becomes "available for use" by the taxpayer (under subsections 13(26) and 13(27)). As analyzed by Canadian SR&ED tax specialists, this provision creates a strong technical argument that capital equipment ordered, paid for, and delivered prior to December 16, 2024 (e.g., in September 2024), but not hooked up, commissioned, or available for use until after December 15, 2024 (e.g., January 2025), is deemed incurred in 2025 for ITC and section 127.1 refundability purposes—though the CRA may initially challenge pre-December 16, 2024 purchase dates.
4.5.2 Software Licences and Accelerated CCA Alternatives (Classes 12 and 50)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), software intended to be incorporated into a commercial product cannot be included in the SR&ED pool, whereas software acquired strictly as a tool to perform SR&ED (such as computer-aided design software) may qualify as a current expense if it benefits only the current fiscal period, or as a capital expenditure if it is of an enduring nature with a useful life exceeding one year. Even where computer hardware or software does not meet the ≥90% ASA SR&ED threshold, Bill C-15 provides immediate write-offs under general Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules: CCA Class 12 (purchased application software) carries a 100% deduction rate; CCA Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data-processing hardware and systems software, normally 55%) receives a 100% first-year immediate deduction under Bill C-15 for property acquired after April 15, 2024 and available for use before 2027; and for other CCA classes, the half-year rule is suspended to provide 3 times the normal first-year deduction for property acquired after 2024 and available for use before 2030 (and 2 times from 2030 through 2033).
4.6 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments (Subsections 127(11.1) and 127(18)–(20))

Money received from governments or clients for R&D work reduces the SR&ED claim dollar-for-dollar under subsections 127(11.1) and 127(18) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act (not subsection 37(2), which deals exclusively with foreign R&D). Under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d), government assistance (grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, and provincial R&D tax credits) and non-government assistance received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received reduce both the section 37(1) deductible pool and qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(11.1).

Furthermore, as confirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in CAE Inc. v. The King (2022 FCA 178), even a repayable, non-forgivable government loan (such as funding under the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative) constitutes "government assistance" that reduces SR&ED qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar by the full principal amount if the loan is provided at below-market interest rates rather than on strictly commercial terms. Similarly, contract payments received or receivable for performing SR&ED on behalf of another person in Canada reduce the contractor's qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar under subsection 127(18). Where assistance involves non-arm's length parties, they may allocate the assistance using Form T1145 under subsection 127(20), and any subsequent repayment of assistance or contract payments generates an ITC in the year of repayment.
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Stacking Mechanics

Nearly all Canadian provinces and Yukon supplement the federal SR&ED program with provincial or territorial R&D tax credits. Because provincial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the federal Income Tax Act, claiming a provincial credit reduces the federal section 37(1) expenditure pool and federal qualified SR&ED expenditures.
5.1 Quebec: The Landmark 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation)

For taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, the Government of Quebec enacted a complete structural overhaul of its provincial R&D tax incentive system, abolishing eight legacy provincial tax measures and replacing them with a single, consolidated, fully refundable tax credit: the CRIC (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation / Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization), administered by Revenu Québec.

items: The Eight Abolished Legacy Quebec Measures: Practitioners must not reference the former 14%–30% Quebec R&D salary tax credit for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. The CRIC replaced and abolished the former R&D Salaries and Wages Tax Credit (14% to 30%), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by Public Research Centres / CCTTs, the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research, the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium, the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services, the Tax Credit for Industrial Design, and the Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Foreign Experts.

Two-Tier Universal Refundable Rate Structure (30% / 20%): The CRIC provides a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified CRIC expenditures exceeding the annual exclusion threshold, and a 20% fully refundable tax credit on all qualified CRIC expenditures in excess of $1,000,000. Unlike the former Quebec regime (which scaled down from 30% to 14% based on corporate assets), the CRIC 30% / 20% refundable rates apply universally to both CCPCs and general/multinational corporations with a permanent establishment in Quebec, regardless of asset size or ownership (though rate reductions can apply in intercompany subcontracting scenarios where >50% of revenue comes from related entities).

Expanded Activity Scope — R&D Plus Pre-Commercialisation: In addition to core R&D, the Quebec CRIC explicitly covers pre-commercialisation activities carried out in Quebec, including regulatory testing and certification processes, product design and industrial design, technological validation, pilot production, and prototype refinement (excluding routine maintenance or improvements on existing systems).

Eligible Cost Categories and Refundability Rates: Qualified CRIC costs include 100% of Quebec employee salaries and wages for eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation work (100% refundable); 100% of capital expenditures (CAPEX) to acquire new depreciable equipment used exclusively in Quebec for eligible activities (100% refundable); and 50% of subcontractor and research contract payments to arm's length R&D contractors, universities, public research centres, CCTTs, and research consortiums (reduced from 80% for universities under the prior regime to a uniform 50% across all subcontractors).

The Dynamic Exclusion Threshold Formula: Before applying the 30% / 20% rates, the claimant must deduct a mandatory annual Exclusion Threshold from its eligible expenditures equal to the greater of: (a) $50,000, OR (b) the sum of the Quebec basic personal amount for each eligible employee for whom CRIC is claimed ($18,571 for 2025; $18,952 for 2026), prorated in proportion to the percentage of time each employee devoted to eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation activities during the year. For example, if a Quebec firm has 10 engineers spending 100% of their time on CRIC activities in 2025, its exclusion threshold is max($50,000, 10 × $18,571) = $185,710; if it has 2 engineers at 100% time ($37,142), the $50,000 floor applies.

Non-Cumulation and Filing Deadline: The CRIC is claimed on the Quebec corporate income tax return filed with Revenu Québec within 12 months after the corporate filing due date (18 months after fiscal year-end), with refunds typically processed within 60 to 90 days. The same expenditure cannot be double-claimed for both the CRIC and another Quebec tax credit such as the C3i (15%–25% tax credit for investment and innovation on manufacturing/IT equipment above $12,500) or the technology integration credit. (KPMG Tax Facts 2025–2026 also notes a 10% non-refundable Quebec R&D tax credit component capped at $1M combined per year with 3-year carryback and 10-year carryforward).

body.text: 5.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC
Ontario offers three complementary R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA and claimed directly on the federal T2 return:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566 / T2SCH566 and T2SCH31): Provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit for corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures per year (maximum annual cash refund of $240,000), shared among associated corporations. Unlike the federal SR&ED limit (which increased to $6M and $15M–$75M under Bill C-15), the Ontario OITC retains its $3,000,000 expenditure limit, which phases out if prior-year federal taxable income of the associated group is between $500,000 and $800,000 OR if prior-year taxable paid-up capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. The Ontario Ministry of Finance updated the OITC rules to confirm that qualified expenditures include 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508 / T2SCH508): Provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (sections 38 to 45 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario)) available to all corporations on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures that qualify for the federal ITC (net of any OITC or OBRITC claimed), with no expenditure cap. Unused ORDTC credits can be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years. Because both the OITC and ORDTC are government assistance that reduces the federal SR&ED pool and federal ITC base, a corporation may file a written waiver with its T2 return to renounce all or part of the ORDTC (or OITC).

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC): Provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred under eligible R&D contracts with Eligible Research Institutes (ERIs) (Ontario universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, and prescribed non-profit research organizations), up to an annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000 shared across an associated group (yielding up to $4,000,000 in annual cash refunds). Payments funding salaries of an ERI employee who is connected to the claimant corporation are excluded.

body.text: 5.3 British Columbia, Alberta, and Western/Atlantic Provinces

In British Columbia, the BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Form T666, sections 97 to 103 of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia)) provides a 10% tax credit on BC qualified SR&ED expenditures. The Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026 (S.B.C. 2026, c. 5) removed the credit's former expiry date (expenditures incurred before September 1, 2027) and aligned it with Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. For CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), the credit is 100% refundable up to the corporation's $6,000,000 expenditure limit (maximum $600,000 cash refund), which for CCPCs phases out as prior-year taxable capital rises from $15,000,000 to $75,000,000, and SR&ED capital expenditures are again eligible. For other corporations or expenditures above the limit, the 10% credit is non-refundable and may be carried back 3 years or carried forward 10 years (or renounced annually). Active corporate members of a partnership can claim their proportionate share, whereas individuals and trusts are excluded.

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970, sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act) is administered separately by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance (Tax and Revenue Administration) rather than the CRA. It provides a fully refundable grant/tax credit on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta R&D expenditures matching federal SR&ED eligibility, structured as an 8% payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base spending level (the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 taxation years) and an enhanced 20% payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the 2-year base spending level.

In Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan R&D Tax Credit (Schedule T2SCH403, sections 63 to 63.4 of The Income Tax Act (Saskatchewan)) provides a 10% refundable tax credit for CCPCs on up to $1,000,000 of eligible Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures (maximum $100,000 annual refund), and a 10% non-refundable credit for CCPC expenditures above $1,000,000 and for all other corporations (carryback 3 years, carryforward 10 years). Saskatchewan's 2026-27 Budget announced, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, an increase in the refundable tier from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 of eligible expenditures and the restoration of eligibility for capital expenditures. In Manitoba, the Manitoba R&D Tax Credit (Schedule T2SCH380, section 7.3 of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba)) provides a 15% tax credit on eligible Manitoba R&D expenditures (including capital expenditures and 100% of contract payments to prescribed Manitoba post-secondary institutions versus 80% for other contracts), which is 100% refundable for R&D performed under contract with a qualifying Manitoba post-secondary institution and 50% refundable (7.5%) / 50% non-refundable (7.5%) for in-house R&D (carryback 3 years, carryforward 20 years, with an option to renounce within 12 months of the T2 filing due date).

In the Atlantic Provinces and Yukon, New Brunswick (section 59 of the New Brunswick Income Tax Act, Schedule T2SCH360), Nova Scotia (section 41 of the Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia), Schedule T2SCH340), and Newfoundland and Labrador (section 42 of the Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador), Schedule T2SCH301 for corporations and Form T1129 for individuals) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit with no expenditure cap. Yukon provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit for corporations and individuals, plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University. Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit.

6.1 Mandatory Prescribed Forms and the May 2026 Bill C-15 Form Releases
To reflect the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the CRA released updated versions of all core SR&ED prescribed forms in May 2026:

items: Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 15, 2026): Part 1 captures general corporate information and the irrevocable Line 160 (Proxy) vs. Line 162 (Traditional) election. Part 2 captures project-by-project technical descriptions (claimants with >20 projects may submit Part 2 for the 20 largest projects in dollar value at filing, retaining the rest for audit). Section A of Part 2 records project title (Line 200), start date (Line 202), completion date (Line 204), and field of science/technology codes. Section B of Part 2 contains the three mandatory technical narrative boxes with strict word limits: Line 242 ("What scientific or technological uncertainties did you attempt to overcome?", maximum 350 words), Line 244 ("What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainties described in line 242?", maximum 700 words, describing hypotheses, experiments/analysis, and results in chronological order), and Line 246 ("What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve or attempt to achieve as a result of the work described in line 244?", maximum 350 words). Section C of Part 2 records key personnel (Lines 253–255), the 10 most expensive post-December 15, 2024 capital properties per project (Lines 262–263), foreign SR&ED (Line 265), and contract work performed on behalf of another party (Line 266). Part 3 computes allowable SR&ED expenditures (Lines 300–390) and the section 37(1) deductible pool (including Line 440 capital disposition proceeds, Line 535 other deductions, and Line 543 s. 127(11.6) non-arm's length cost adjustments). Part 4 computes qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes (including Line 502 PPA and Line 504 25% First-Term / 25% Second-Term SUE). Part 5 computes the Salary Base (applying the 75% / 2.5 × YMPE cap) and the 55% PPA (Line 820). Part 6 breaks down project costs (Part 6A Box 759 for post-Dec 15, 2024 equipment leases; Part 6B Boxes 780, 782, 786 for the 20 most expensive capital properties; Part 6C Boxes 788, 790, 792 for the 20 most expensive SUE properties). Part 7 and Part 8 contain statistical disclosures and the mandatory claim documentation checklist. Part 9 and Part 10 contain mandatory claim preparer disclosures (Lines 935, 970, 975) and certification.

Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, updated May 22, 2026) or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)): Mandatory prescribed form required under paragraph 127(9)(m) to claim the ITC.

Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, updated May 29, 2026): Allocates the $6,000,000 expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.3).
Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026): Allocates assistance under subsection 127(20).
