body.text: 6.2 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline (Subsection 37(11) and Paragraph 127(9)(m))

One of the most unforgiving provisions in Canadian tax law is the SR&ED reporting deadline. Subsection 37(11) (and subsection 37(12)) governs the deadline for filing Form T661 to claim SR&ED expenditures, while paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) governs the deadline for filing Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) to claim the ITC. (Section 230 of the Income Tax Act governs general books and records retention, not the SR&ED filing deadline). Under both subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m), the taxpayer must file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, a corporation has exactly 18 months from its taxation year-end (6 months + 12 months) to file a complete Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31.

The 18-month deadline is a strict statutory bar: there is no statutory mechanism, appeal, or ministerial discretion to extend it. Taxpayer relief under subsection 220(3.1) applies only to penalties and interest and cannot revive a late SR&ED claim. If a claimant files Form T661 on time at 18 months but forgets to attach Schedule T2SCH31 until 47 days later (Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 301), or files Form T661 on time but leaves technical narrative boxes blank (Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2018 FCA 57), the ITC is permanently forfeited. Even where a claimant files early and the CRA identifies missing details during a review, any missing prescribed information must be received by the CRA within the original 18-month window.
6.3 Claim Preparer Penalties (Subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3)) and Criminal Fraud Sanctions (Subsection 239(1.1))

Since January 1, 2014, every SR&ED claimant must complete Part 9 of Form T661 disclosing whether a "claim preparer" participated in preparing Form T661, including the preparer's name, Business Number or Social Insurance Number (collected under section 237), billing arrangement (contingency fee vs. flat/hourly rate), and total fee. Even if no external claim preparer assisted with the claim, the claimant must still complete Lines 935, 970, and 975 in Part 9. Under subsection 162(5.1) (subject to the due diligence defence in subsection 162(5.2) and definitions in subsection 162(5.3)), if required claim preparer information in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty applies (for which the claimant and claim preparer are jointly and severally liable), though the SR&ED claim itself is not disallowed for this reason.

At the criminal enforcement level, under paragraphs 239(1.1)(a) and (c) of the Income Tax Act, making, participating in, or acquiescing in false or misleading representations or fabricated entries in an SR&ED claim is a criminal offence punishable on summary conviction by a fine of between 50% and 200% of the excess ITC claimed or obtained, plus up to 2 years imprisonment. As established in R. v. Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc., Maged Elhami, and Shady Elhami (2017 QCCQ 2684), the 50%–200% fine applies to the fraudulent credit claimed on the return even if the CRA rejected the file during audit and paid out $0.
6.4 CRA Review Process, Service Standards, April 2026 Pre-Claim Approval, and Dispute Resolution

In the CRA's most recent published fiscal year, out of 24,160 SR&ED claims filed (23,677 processed, allowing $4.6 billion out of $4.9 billion claimed), 90% of claims were accepted as filed, 6% were accepted with modifications, and 4% were denied. The CRA's published processing service standards are 60 calendar days for claims accepted as filed (met 95% of the time in the most recent year against a 90% target) and 180 calendar days for refundable claims selected for review (met 92.5% of the time against a 90% target; no published day-count standard exists for non-refundable claims under review).

In January 2026, the CRA ended its legacy Pre-Claim Consultation service and, in April 2026, launched a formal Pre-Claim Approval process. Under Pre-Claim Approval, a corporation with gross business income under $25,000,000 can ask the CRA before filing to determine whether up to three SR&ED projects are technically eligible; the CRA issues a determination within 8 weeks, which is valid for up to 3 years and limits any post-filing review strictly to financial expenditures.

When a post-filing claim is selected for review (managed in the CRA's CORTAX and AIMS systems), a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) evaluates technical eligibility and a Financial Reviewer (FR) examines claimed expenditures. Claimants must retain contemporaneous evidence answering four questions—What work was done, Who was involved, When they did it, and How expenditures were calculated—supported by the Part 8 Form T661 Checklist (project planning docs, time sheets, design of experiments, lab notebooks, system architecture, source code, trial run logs, test data/conclusions, meeting minutes, photographs/videos, prototypes/scrap, and contracts). Practitioners advise avoiding nine major audit red flags: (1) retroactively reconstructed records; (2) identical round-number time allocations across staff; (3) marketing-style narratives with zero failed hypotheses; (4) expenditures disproportionate to the technical story; (5) contractor invoices claimed whole without isolating SR&ED or applying the 80% factor; (6) support work claimed without satisfying the commensurate test; (7) shared equipment/facilities claimed at 100%; (8) subjective uncertainty based on internal knowledge gaps; and (9) disorganized submissions.

If a disagreement arises during review, the claimant escalates first to the RTA / FR, second to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) / Financial Review Manager (FRM), and third—within the 30-day proposal period before the file closes—requests an Administrative Review using the prescribed form (which reviews due process and compliance with legislation/policy rather than conducting a second technical review). Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is mailed, the corporation has 90 days under paragraph 165(1)(b) to serve a Notice of Objection (with an absolute statutory outer limit of 1 year and 90 days to seek an extension under subsections 166.1(7) and 166.2(5), as strictly enforced in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 146). Finally, if appealing to the Tax Court of Canada, claimants with claims exceeding $12,000 per year must file under the General Procedure, because electing the Informal Procedure caps additional refundable ITC relief at $12,000 per taxation year under section 18.1 of the Tax Court of Canada Act (1726437 Ontario Inc. o/a Airmax Technologies v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 376).
7. Comprehensive Analysis of Leading Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence

Canadian SR&ED tax law is heavily shaped by the jurisprudence of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA). The following subsections synthesize the leading Canadian judicial precedents through late 2025/2026.
7.1 The Foundational Five-Criteria Test and Appellate Endorsements

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, [1998] T.C.J. No. 340, T.C.C., Docket 97-531(IT)G, May 1, 1998, per Judge Bowman), the taxpayer constructed physical scale hydraulic models to resolve complex fluid dynamics and sediment transport uncertainties. Judge Bowman allowed the appeal in part and articulated at paragraph 16 the seminal Five Criteria for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED under subsection 248(1): (1) Was there a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures accessible to competent professionals in the field? (2) Did the claimant formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty (following a five-stage process of observation, clear objective, articulation of uncertainty, formulation of hypotheses, and methodical testing)? (3) Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including trained and systematic observation, measurement, experiment, and modification of hypotheses? (4) Did the process result in a technological advancement in general understanding (noting that rejection of a hypothesis is itself a technological advance because it eliminates a possible solution)? (5) Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed?

In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 D.T.C. 5087, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1890, F.C.A., Docket A-710-96, December 21, 1998, per Robertson J.A.), the appellant funded the development of a cast-in-situ concrete forming panel ("spatial membrane") by engineer Leonid Slonimsky and businessman Daniel Dorcich, producing a working prototype in 1983 and a Canadian patent in 1991. Because Slonimsky died before trial and his Georgetown test records were not produced, the Tax Court dismissed the claim on the ground that the taxpayer lacked written test logs enabling third-party "repeatability" (Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R., 88 D.T.C. 1363), despite finding as a fact that engineering uncertainty, hypothesis testing, and a patented technological advance had occurred. The Federal Court of Appeal unanimously reversed the Tax Court and allowed the appeal with costs, holding that: (a) expert witnesses only provide "prescription glasses" to assist the judge on technical facts; (b) research need not succeed to qualify as SR&ED; and (c) while contemporaneous documentary evidence is the most reliable proof of systematic research, where a taxpayer has a plausible reason for missing records and proves that an actual technological advancement was achieved, the court may infer that systematic research was conducted without imposing an absolute third-party repeatability bar.
Subsequent Federal Court of Appeal decisions have consistently enforced Northwest Hydraulic:

items: C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen (2001 FCA 393, Docket A-601-00, December 11, 2001, per Sexton J.A.): Affirmed the dismissal of 1991–1995 SR&ED claims for developing the "International Distributed Lottery System" (IDLS) software handling 25,000 daily orders; while having a commercial goal does not exclude a project, the Crown's expert (Dr. Takagaki) proved all challenges were resolvable via routine software engineering, and the appellant failed to retain contemporaneous project records or call its project manager to testify.

Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2010 TCC 319, Docket 2008-3875(IT)G, June 11, 2010, aff'd 2011 FCA 355, 2012 D.T.C. 5031, Docket A-222-11, December 15, 2011): Affirmed the dismissal of 2005 SR&ED claims for developing a lighter "Multi-Bin" storage system (20 cubic feet per square metre capacity and 100-lb load limit), holding that comparative load testing of plastic resins and aluminum and using a thermoforming heat sink constituted routine engineering and standard procedures.

Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 246, Docket 2016-4880(IT)G, October 30, 2019, per Owen J., aff'd 2021 FCA 88, Docket A-442-19, May 10, 2021, per Webb J.A.): Dismissed the appellant's 2009–2010 claims for designing curved tempered-glass memorial niche columns using 3D CAD modelling and factory mock-ups, and squarely rejected the appellant's legal argument that Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 3 ("scientific method") went beyond the text of subsection 248(1), confirming that Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, Jentel Manufacturing, and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada (2016 FCA 152) are binding law.

body.text: 7.2 Software Development, System Uncertainty, Post-Release Failure, and Evidence Cases

In National R&D Inc. v. The Queen (2020 TCC 47, Docket 2017-3837(IT)G, July 7, 2020, per Lafleur J.), an SR&ED consulting firm claimed $68,029 in 2011 SR&ED expenditures ($23,810 ITC; $42,284.54 agreed expenses if eligible) for developing an internal web-based "Project Tracking System" (PTS Project) using legacy tools already known to its staff (ADO, Classic ASP, COM+, and SQL Server 2000). Justice Lafleur dismissed the appeal with costs, holding that even with the company's president (Mr. Amit Saini, P.Eng., CPA) testifying as a "litigant expert," project timelines and task spreadsheets that merely tracked hours spent, coupled with unversioned source code snippets lacking revision histories, failed to demonstrate formulated hypotheses or a "logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests" under Northwest Hydraulic criteria 3, 4, and 5.
Conversely, the Tax Court has strongly upheld taxpayer claims where genuine system uncertainty or post-release failure was proven with credible evidence:

items: A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen (2019 TCC 48, Docket 2014-3465(IT)G, February 28, 2019, per Russell J.): An Ontario precision machining firm claimed $1,212,213 in ITCs across 2006–2008 ($827,348, $1,202,398, and $789,579 in current expenditures plus $431,259, $555,984, and $346,579 in Shared-Use-Equipment) for building custom 80-ton, 60-ton, and 40-ton horizontal CNC "Matteo" lathes (Project #4) and a fabricated-bed double-wheel roll grinding machine (Project #6) that was ultimately abandoned due to severe spindle vibration. Justice Russell allowed the ITCs in full for Project #6 across all three years (confirming that abandoning a failed project after systematic vibration testing fully qualifies) and allowed Project #4 in full for 2007 and one-third for 2008 based on system uncertainty in integrating complex subsystems at extreme tolerances (while denying the 2006 claim for repairing Italian Tacchi lathes for lack of evidence).

1726437 Ontario Inc. o/a Airmax Technologies v. The Queen (2012 TCC 376, Docket 2010-3660(IT)I, October 25, 2012, per Hogan J.): Held that integrating a European boiler, reprogrammed Korean ECM fan motors, and perforated flexible ductwork to reduce high-velocity residential HVAC noise from 60 dB to 40 dB involved genuine system integration uncertainty under IC 86-4R3 para. 4.8, validating $387,553 in disputed 2007–2008 SR&ED expenditures (though the taxpayer's Informal Procedure election capped additional 2008 refundable ITC relief at $12,000 under section 18.1 of the Tax Court of Canada Act).

6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 77, Docket 2012-3634(IT)G, March 31, 2015, per D'Auray J.): Led by miniaturization expert Raja Tuli, the appellant developed a 1.5" × 1.5" × 10" wireless portable printer, commercially released 200 units in late 2008, and suffered >20% customer failures (curled paper and battery drain after 5–10 pages), prompting it to pull the product and claim $103,628 (2009) and $49,688 (2010) in SR&ED ITCs. Justice D'Auray allowed the appeal with costs, ruling that premature commercial release does not end technological uncertainty when real-world deployment reveals unresolved system-level technological defects, and accepted on a balance of probabilities that the 2010 technical report was filed on time with the stamped T2 return.

Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 21, Jan 31, 2017, per Boyle J.), Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6, Jan 17, 2017, per Sommerfeldt J.), Murray Arlin Dentistry Professional Corporation v. The Queen (2012 TCC 133, Apr 24, 2012, per Woods J.), and Highland Foundry Ltd. v. The Queen (94 D.T.C. 1725, Aug 15, 1994, per McArthur J.): In Life Choice, natural health product formulations developed on paper via literature reviews without physical/clinical testing failed subsection 248(1). In Joel Theatrical Rigging, shop-floor rigging tests for hydraulic fire curtains and manual overrides failed for lack of contemporaneous notes/drawings or engineering testimony. In Murray Arlin Dentistry, $103,950/yr claims based on push-button Tritan dental implant software queries and unsubstantiated 20% salary estimates were dismissed. In Highland Foundry, $205,083 in 1985–1987 capital costs for a patented prototype green-sand refiner later used in production were allowed because the 90% ASA test applied during research prosecution without commercial hindsight.

body.text: 7.3 Government Assistance, Strict Filing Deadlines, Discovery Undertakings, and Criminal Fraud Precedents

In Her Majesty the Queen v. CCLC Technologies Inc. (96 D.T.C. 6527, [1996] F.C.J. No. 1226, F.C.A., Docket A-801-95, September 19, 1996, per Strayer J.A.) and CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2022 FCA 178, Docket A-264-21, October 19, 2022, per Boivin J.A., aff'g 2021 TCC 57), the Federal Court of Appeal established that government funding under non-commercial terms—including Alberta's Coal Research Agreement in CCLC Technologies and Industry Canada's repayable, below-market-interest SADI loan for "Project Falcon" in CAE Inc.—constitutes government assistance under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(11.1) that reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures by the full principal amount.
On strict statutory filing and objection deadlines, the courts have uniformly enforced the statutory bars in subsection 37(11), paragraph 127(9)(m), and subsection 166.2(5):

items: Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 211, aff'd 2016 FCA 301, Docket A-432-15, November 28, 2016, per Nadon J.A.): Filing a completed Form T661 on the June 30, 2010 deadline (18 months after the December 31, 2008 year-end) did not excuse filing Schedule T2SCH31 47 days late on August 16, 2010; section 32 of the Interpretation Act did not apply, and the ITC on $95,791 of recognized SR&ED expenditures was permanently barred under paragraph 127(9)(m).

Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 9, aff'd 2018 FCA 57, Docket A-61-17, March 21, 2018, per Woods J.A.) and 1373744 Ontario Inc. o/a One Source Metal v. The Queen (2009 TCC 511, Docket 2008-3566(IT)I, October 14, 2009, per Bowie J.): In Westsource, leaving Boxes 240, 242, and 244 blank on Form T661 for a continuing project violated subsection 37(11) even though an associated company's claim for the same project was accepted. In One Source Metal, where the courier's file copies of the 2005–2006 T661 forms bore a March 28, 2007 CRA stamp (before the March 31, 2007 deadline) but the technical report bore no stamp and was faxed April 12, 2007, the claim was barred under subsection 37(11).

Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 146, Docket 2024-842(IT)APP, October 14, 2025, per Ouimet J.): Applying the four-step proof-of-mailing framework under subsections 244(14), 244(15), and paragraph 248(7)(a), Justice Ouimet held that CRA affidavits proving automated BCCS print-to-mail delivery on September 13, 2022 triggered the non-rebuttable presumption of receipt and barred the taxpayer's January 18, 2024 objection extension request (filed past the December 12, 2023 1-year-and-90-day cutoff) under subsection 166.2(5).

Fio Corporation v. The Queen (2014 TCC 58, Docket 2012-1452(IT)G, February 20, 2014, per D'Arcy J.) and R. v. Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc., Maged Elhami, and Shady Elhami (2017 QCCQ 2684, Docket 500-73-004048-134, March 27, 2017, per Tremblay J.C.Q.): In Fio Corporation, the Tax Court held that the implied undertaking rule prohibits the CRA from using pre-trial discovery binders to issue new reassessments without prior leave of the Court, enjoining the Crown and awarding $25,000 in costs to the appellant. In Tempora, submitting $4.5M+ in fabricated Pyro Genesis subcontractor invoices to claim $1,324,294 in SR&ED ITCs resulted in convictions under subsections 239(1.1)(a) and (c) and criminal fines of $1,324,294 against each of the three co-defendants ($3,972,882 total) despite the CRA having disbursed $0.

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839
Definition of SR&ED under s. 248(1) and IC 86-4R3
Taxpayer won (in part): Established the 5 Criteria for SR&ED; rejected hypotheses still advance technology.
Evidentiary standard for "repeatability" when test records are lost
Taxpayer won: Reversed TCC; rejected rigid third-party repeatability requirement where patented advancement was proven.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393
Custom lottery software (IDLS) vs. routine software engineering
Crown won: Standard software engineering and absence of contemporaneous records/witnesses defeated claim.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355
Thermoforming storage bins & material load testing
Crown won: Testing standard plastic/aluminum materials and heat sinks was routine engineering.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88
Crown won: Confirmed Northwest Hydraulic's scientific method requirement is binding law interpreting s. 248(1).
National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47
Legacy software development, time sheets & unversioned code
Crown won: Time sheets and code snippets without recorded hypotheses or logical test progression fail criteria 3–5.
A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 48
System uncertainty in 80-ton CNC lathes & abandoned grinder
Split / Taxpayer won core claims: Validated system uncertainty and confirmed abandoned failed R&D qualifies.
1726437 Ontario Inc. (Airmax) v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 376
HVAC system integration uncertainty & Informal Procedure cap
Taxpayer won on merits: $387,553 qualified as SR&ED, but Informal Procedure election capped relief at $12,000.
6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 77
Post-commercial-release R&D after >20% field failure rate
Taxpayer won: Commercial release of 200 mini-printers did not end uncertainty when real-world system defects emerged.
Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 21
Theoretical natural health formulations without physical testing
Crown won: Literature reviews and paper formulations without physical/clinical experimentation cannot qualify as SR&ED.
Joel Theatrical Rigging v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6
Crown won: Retrospective consultant schedules and lack of engineering testimony or contemporaneous logs failed onus.
Murray Arlin Dentistry PC v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 133
Clinical dental implant database tracking & time estimates
Crown won: Push-button software queries and unsubstantiated 20% salary estimates failed to prove systematic research.
Highland Foundry Ltd. v. The Queen, 94 D.T.C. 1725
Prototype sand refiner subsequently used in foundry production
Taxpayer won: ASA (90%) test evaluated during research prosecution, not retroactively via commercial hindsight.
Government coal research funding with non-commercial return
Crown won: Non-commercial government funding constitutes "government assistance" under s. 127(9) & s. 127(11.1).
Repayable SADI government loan at below-market interest rate
Crown won: Full principal of below-market repayable government loan is "government assistance" reducing SR&ED ITCs.
Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 301
Timely Form T661 but late Schedule T2SCH31 (past 18 months)
Crown won: Filing T661 on time does not cure late filing of Schedule 31 under paragraph 127(9)(m); ITC barred.
Westsource Group Holdings v. The Queen, 2018 FCA 57
Form T661 filed on time with Boxes 240, 242, 244 left blank
Crown won: Leaving technical narrative boxes blank violates subsection 37(11) "prescribed information" requirement.
Simon Ribbans Photography v. The King, 2025 TCC 146
Late Notice of Objection past 1-year-and-90-day statutory cutoff
Crown won: CRA proof of mailing triggered non-rebuttable receipt under s. 248(7)(a); extension barred under s. 166.2(5).
CRA using Tax Court discovery binders to issue new reassessments
Taxpayer won motion: Implied undertaking rule bars CRA from using discovery documents for new reassessments ($25K costs).
Fabricated $4.5M subcontractor invoices ($0 paid out by CRA)
Crown won conviction: Each of 3 defendants fined $1,324,294 under ITA s. 239(1.1) despite $0 payout.
